segments.narration: The oldest map of America was drawn with modern paint. Yale unveiled it in 1965, a day before Columbus Day, showing Vinland southwest of Greenland.
Paul Mellon had bought it for roughly three hundred thousand dollars and donated it, on one condition: total secrecy until the scholars published.
It looked unbeatable. So why did chemist after chemist keep finding a pigment no medieval scribe could possibly have owned?
The ink held anatase, a titanium dioxide manufactured only from the 1920s onward. Walter McCrone's team flagged it back in 1972.
Yale settled it in 2021. Titanium everywhere, almost no iron gall ink, and modern writing added to the real medieval manuscript bound beside it.

verdicts.claim: Yale's 2021 analysis found high titanium and almost no iron gall ink, plus modern ink alterations to the genuine Tartar Relation bound with the map.
verdicts.note: The Yale 2021 announcement reports titanium and barium in the ink, little to no iron, sulfur or copper versus genuine 15th-century comparators, and infrared evidence of modern ink altering the Tartar Relation.
